allometry.title: Allometry
allometry.info: Organs do not scale 1:1 with body mass. On a log-log plot the slope is the scaling exponent — lungs near 1, brains shallower, bones steeper. Drag mass and watch each organ ride its own line.

aspect-ratio.title: Aspect Ratio
aspect-ratio.info: Wingspan² / wing area. High AR soars cheap (albatross); low AR turns tight (sparrow). Drag span and chord; L/D updates. Ikran sits between soarer and agile hunter.

biomechanics.title: Biomechanics
biomechanics.info: Forces through a living machine. Tap a banshee joint to see torque arrows; ground reaction force spikes on landing. Structure is the answer to load.

cursorial.title: Cursorial
cursorial.info: Built to run. Limb length ratio sets the gait: walk → trot → gallop as Froude number climbs. Stretch the legs and the phase diagram shifts.

dynamic-soaring.title: Dynamic Soaring
dynamic-soaring.info: Harvest a wind gradient: climb into faster air, dive downwind, bank, repeat. Energy bar fills from shear, not muscle. Toggle soaring vs flapping cost.

ecomorph.title: Ecomorph
ecomorph.info: Form following niche. Six silhouettes for six habitats — pick a habitat and the matching body plan lights. Convergence writes the same answer twice.

froude-number.title: Froude Number
froude-number.info: v / √(gL) — inertial over gravitational. Near Fr ≈ 1 wave drag peaks and gaits shift. Push speed through the canal; watch the meter and the bow wave.

isometry.title: Isometry
isometry.info: Same shape, bigger size. Scale the twin up and wall thickness stays proportional — volume outruns cross-section, so pure isometry snaps bones. Nature refuses it.

kleibers-law.title: Kleiber's Law
kleibers-law.info: Metabolic rate scales ~mass^¾, not 1. Log-log, life sits on a shallow line. Drag mass for a Pandoran body; it should fall near Kleiber's slope.

leading-edge-vortex.title: Leading-Edge Vortex
leading-edge-vortex.info: A rolling vortex glued to the wing's front edge boosts lift at high angle — insect and banshee trick. Toggle attached flow vs LEV and watch the low-pressure core.

lift.title: Lift
lift.info: Aerofoil + angle of attack. Streamlines pack above, pressure drops, net force up — until stall. Sweep AoA; Cl rises then collapses.

pneumatic-bone.title: Pneumatic Bone
pneumatic-bone.info: Hollow, strutted, air-filled. Slide from solid to pneumatic: mass falls faster than stiffness. Flyers buy span with emptiness.

power-curve.title: Power Curve
power-curve.info: Power required vs speed is a U: slow costs hover-work, fast costs parasite drag. Markers shift with wing loading and mass — min-power and max-range speeds.

quadrupedal-launch.title: Quadrupedal Launch
quadrupedal-launch.info: Big flyers push with all four limbs. Step the banshee sequence: crouch → vault → unfold → first stroke. Power comes from the leap, not the first flap alone.

quetzalcoatlus.title: Quetzalcoatlus
quetzalcoatlus.info: Earth's giant azhdarchid beside ikran. Compare span and mass; the plausibility meter separates supported loads from fantasy overload.

reynolds-number.title: Reynolds Number
reynolds-number.info: ρvL/μ — inertia over viscosity. Tiny/slow = smooth laminar streaks; big/fast = turbulent chaos. Pandora's dense air shifts the Re of a given wing.

scaling-exponent.title: Scaling Exponent
scaling-exponent.info: Trait ∝ base^b. Pick b (½, ¾, 1, 2) and watch the log-log curve tilt. Geometry and metabolism live on different slopes.

square-cube-law.title: Square–Cube Law
square-cube-law.info: Scale a body by k: area ×k², volume ×k³. Surface loses the race — heat dump, bone stress, muscle force all feel the mismatch. Grow the cube until volume overtops area.

thermal-soaring.title: Thermal Soaring
thermal-soaring.info: Sun-heated ground lofts invisible columns. Ikran circles inside a thermal and gains height for free. Place a thermal; watch the climb.

wing-loading.title: Wing Loading
wing-loading.info: Weight / wing area. High loading = fast landing, poor turns; low loading = floaty and agile. Match ikran's preset or invent your own flyer.

tandem-wing.title: The cost of a second wing
tandem-wing.subtitle: Slide the rear wing up and back. Watch which move actually helps.
tandem-wing.dragStrip: Drag to hold the same weight up
tandem-wing.staggerLabel: How far back the rear wing sits
tandem-wing.dragNote: Compared with a single wing of the same total span

hint.spoiled: Stacked almost level, the two wings sit in each other's air and spoil each other badly. This is the arrangement that looks most like a second pair of wings — and it is the one that wastes the most.
hint.partial: Lifting the rear wing clear of the wake recovers much of the loss. Notice that sliding it backwards barely changes the drag at all: it is the vertical separation doing the work, not the fore-and-aft one.
hint.cleared: With a wide vertical gap the two surfaces barely feel each other. The drag is close to the best a pair of wings can manage — still nowhere near what one long wing of the same total span would achieve.

aftNote.spoiled: Flying in air already pushed downward

aria.spoiled: Two wings almost level with each other, the rear wing deep in the front wing's downward-deflected wake, losing most of its lift.
aria.partial: The rear wing raised partly clear of the front wing's wake, recovering some lift.
aria.cleared: The rear wing well above the front wing's wake, meeting almost undisturbed air.

wing-phase.title: Timing two pairs of wings
wing-phase.subtitle: A four-winged flyer chooses when the back pair beats. That choice is the whole trick.
wing-phase.psiLabel: How far the rear pair lags

hint.together: Both pairs beating as one gives the hardest single shove — how a dragonfly launches, or breaks away from something chasing it. It also costs the most, because all four wings fight the same air at the same instant.
hint.recapture: A quarter-beat behind, the rear pair flies through the swirling air the front pair threw off and takes some of that energy back. Measured on real dragonflies, this timing is the cheapest way to cruise.
hint.counter: Beating in opposition, the two pairs cancel each other's shoves and the body stops bouncing. Peak lift is the lowest of the three, but the animal becomes a steady platform — which matters if you are aiming at something.

aria.together: Both wing pairs beating in unison, producing the largest peak lift and the highest power cost.
aria.recapture: The rear wing pair beating a quarter-cycle behind the front pair, crossing its shed swirl and recovering energy from it.
aria.counter: The wing pairs beating in opposition, cancelling body movement for a steady platform.

static-margin.title: The bargain every flyer strikes
static-margin.subtitle: Move the centre of mass. Stability and agility sit at opposite ends of one dial.
static-margin.cgLabel: Where the mass sits along the body

disturbance.stable: A gust lifts the nose — the body pushes it back down
disturbance.neutral: A gust lifts the nose — the body simply stays there
disturbance.relaxed: A gust lifts the nose — and the body keeps going

hint.stable: With the mass well forward the flyer rights itself after every disturbance, which is restful and safe — and the same restoring force fights every turn the animal actually wants to make.
hint.neutral: Balanced on the knife edge. Nothing pushes the nose back, and nothing pushes it further. The body goes where it is put and stays there.
hint.relaxed: Past the balance point the flyer no longer rights itself: a nudge grows instead of fading. The nose now swings far faster than any stable body could manage, at the price of needing constant correction. Fighter designers chose this deliberately.

aria.stable: The centre of mass sits well ahead of the point a gust acts on, so the body rights itself and resists commanded turns.
aria.neutral: The centre of mass sits at the point a gust acts on, neither righting nor diverging.
aria.relaxed: The centre of mass sits behind the point a gust acts on, so disturbances grow and the body pitches very quickly.

turn-envelope.title: How hard can it turn?
turn-envelope.subtitle: Two walls bound every turn: running out of lift, and running out of body.

hint.lift: Down here the wing is the limit — pull any harder and it stalls. Every extra scrap of speed buys a tighter turn, right up to the corner.
hint.structure: Past the corner the wing could pull harder but the body cannot take it. From here on, more speed only makes the circle wider.

aria.lift: The operating point sits on the lift-limited edge of the turn envelope, below corner speed.
aria.structure: The operating point sits on the structural limit of the turn envelope, above corner speed.
